# Draft message to a possible half-sister

I've written a draft, but it doesn't say "I think you're my half-sister." Here's why, followed by the draft.

## Why the draft doesn't say "half-sister"

- **A first message is effectively final.** If she is a half-sibling, it could reveal that a parent had a child she doesn't know about. That can disrupt her family, and you can't take it back. The usual practice for possible parents and half-siblings is to give only facts and let the recipient work out the relationship herself.
- **The DNA alone may not show a half-sibling.** The amount of DNA half-siblings share also fits a grandparent, an aunt or niece, or a double first cousin. I haven't seen your match data, so I can't tell which of these fit. If you say "half-sister" and it's actually one of the others, the mistake is very hard to undo.

If you still want the direct version after reading this, tell me and I'll write it. I'd advise against it.

## Draft

> Hi [her username on the site],
>
> My name is [your first name]. I'm writing about the DNA match between my kit, "[your kit name]", and the kit "[her kit name/username]" on [testing site]. If you manage this kit for someone else, I'd be grateful if you could pass this on.
>
> I was born in [place] in [year]. [Optional, only if you're comfortable sharing it: I'm trying to learn more about my [father's / mother's] side of the family.]
>
> Our match is a close one, and I'd like to understand how we're connected. Would you be willing to tell me which side of your family you think this match comes through, your mother's or your father's?
>
> I know messages like this can come out of the blue. Please take whatever time you need. If you'd rather not reply, I understand.
>
> Best wishes,
> [first name]

The shared cM and segment numbers are deliberately left out. At half-sibling levels they would hint at the relationship, and she can see them on the site anyway. Fill in only what you can actually see on the site. Don't estimate anything.

## Before you send

- **Who tested?** Is the kit yours, or do you manage it for someone else? If someone else tested, that person has to agree to the contact and decide what can be shared, and they should be the one to send it.
- **How it reaches her.** Use the testing site's messaging or a contact route you already have. Don't search for her email, phone number or social media.
- **Take screenshots first.** Save dated screenshots of the match entry (kit names, shared cM, longest segment) and any tree linked to it. Keep them on your own device. Matches sometimes hide their profile or tree after being contacted.
- **Privacy check for the message.** Before you send it, write down:
  - whose details it contains
  - which fields you're sharing (birth place and year, the family side)
  - that it goes to her through [site]
  - who else might see it, such as a kit manager or the person who owns her account

  Also note whether either of you lives where data-protection rules apply, such as the EU or UK GDPR.
- **A published template.** Leah Larkin's "Letter to a Birth Parent" ([The DNA Geek, 2017](https://thednageek.com/letter-to-a-birth-parent/)) is a good model for this kind of message. I haven't read it here, so read it yourself before borrowing from it.

## If she doesn't reply

Write it down as "no response as of [date]", not as a refusal. Don't send follow-ups or more direct messages. Better options are a second cousin on the same side, asked only about family-tree facts, or a fresh message after at least a year.

>
> The site shows we share **[X] cM**, with a longest segment of **[Y] cM**. That's a close match, and I'm trying to understand how we're connected.
>
